prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of atoms, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a single, clearly bounded achievement with a clean chain from idea to result: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated at once, and the resulting systems reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 in several independent laboratories. The consequences are concrete and already demonstrated, including centimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, tight bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, and the evidence base for a redefinition of the second. The credit also divides in a way I can defend: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for taking accuracy, coherence and systematic control to the frontier and tying the clock to the comb infrastructure. A two-name prize is compact and leaves no obvious omitted founder within the supplied credit. I weigh it above the other candidates because it is mature, reproducible and already used as a measuring instrument by other fields, not only a platform for future promise.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is proximity to earlier recognition: the frequency comb (2005) and ion-trap control with the ion clock (2012) mean some colleagues may read lattice clocks as a continuation rather than a new discovery. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the headline application is still prospective, and there is a real attribution question about how much of the 1e-18 record belongs to Ye's group versus other groups (JILA/NIST, PTB, RIKEN and elsewhere) that are outside the two supplied names. I also have to guard against my own taste: a laser-spectroscopist will naturally value a measurement breakthrough, and that is not the same as the broadest scientific impact.

responses.point: Pearce ranks Kane, Mele and Molenkamp first, arguing that the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulator are original, clearly confirmed experimentally, and broad in reach, with a timely recognition after more than fifteen years of independent confirmation.
responses.response: I agree that B042 is one of the strongest conceptual candidates and that the experimental confirmation is excellent, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. My disagreement is about the credit and the recent record. Several of you, including Johansson, Mehlig and Lindroth, noted that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu are decisive and are not in the credited trio, and with Zhang deceased the allocation cannot be repaired by simply widening the prize. The 2016 prize also already honoured topological phases, so the novelty argument is not stronger here than for the clocks. B037 has a cleaner attribution to two living people and a tighter experimental chain, and I would not trade that for a broader but contestable credit set.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the ATLAS and CMS Higgs observation first because the 2013 prize recognised the mechanism while the observation itself has no prize, and he calls it fully mature, while admitting that the three supplied names are founders and project leaders and cannot represent the collaborations.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously; the discovery is clearly Nobel-grade and the missing observation prize is a real argument. But I do not see how we can responsibly write a three-person citation for a discovery by two collaborations of thousands. Choosing Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee would credit proposers and project leadership rather than the analyses that produced the result, and the committee would be defending that allocation for years. I would be more open if someone can show a defensible, rule-compliant formulation that centres on the detector concepts; until then I rank the clock higher because its credit is unambiguous. I note Danielsson himself ranks B037 second, so we may agree on the clocks as a fallback.

responses.point: Olsson ranks solid-state femtosecond lasers first, citing broad impact on spectroscopy and microscopy and the link to the 2023 attosecond prize, and she places B037 fourth, noting that the pending redefinition of the second may favour waiting a little.
responses.response: The femtosecond laser case is good and very practical, and I agree that Ti:sapphire and mode-locking sit under much of modern ultrafast and comb technology. I disagree on waiting for the redefinition: the prize is for the physics and the demonstrated accuracy, and the lattice clocks are already beyond the caesium standard in multiple independent laboratories. A formal redefinition is a metrological decision that follows the science, not a precondition for it. On B004 my reservation is the one you flag yourself, that priority around Kerr-lens mode-locking is not fully settled, so the three-way split looks harder to defend than the two-way split for the clocks.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks lattice clocks first, stressing that the atomic-structure physics of magic wavelengths and clock shifts is clean, that the credit supports a compact two-person prize, and that recognition may even be overdue given the 2005 and 2012 prizes on adjacent topics.
responses.response: I largely agree, and her atomic-structure view strengthens the case that the achievement is a controlled, well-understood effect rather than a fortunate empirical result. Where I would qualify her point is that the adjacent prizes cut both ways: a colleague may say the field has already been rewarded twice, so our citation should be written narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime rather than around clocks in general. Her second-ranked B018 is the main rival in her ballot; I regard it as promising but less settled because the superconducting mechanism is still debated.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or as an incremental extension.

How to describe Ye's contribution in the citation, as the lattice clock itself or as the comb-clock integration and accuracy frontier, and whether other groups' priority on specific 1e-18 results needs to be reflected.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a reason to wait or as confirmation that the work is mature.
Whether B042 or B018 will carry enough broad support that a clock prize looks like a narrower choice by comparison.
statement.conflict_note: I trained in laser spectroscopy at Lund under Sune Svanberg and spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory; the 2005 prize to Hall and Hansch is cited as adjacent to this candidate, so I disclose that connection and field proximity. My profile documents no collaboration, funding link or institutional tie with Katori or Ye, and my later work on quantum memories and WACQT is nearer to B008 and B016 than to B037. Beyond this proximity, no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile, though the committee may wish to weigh my disclosed closeness to the field.
